1.pericope_label: I love the Lord, because he hath heard my voice and my supplications. Because he hath inclined his ear unto me, therefore will I call upon him as long as I live

schools.summary: Augustine presses the logic of the received reading. Is it a reason for having loved that the Lord will hear, when we should rather love because he has heard? He answers that hope is wont to inflame love, and then asks how the soul knows that God has inclined his ear at all except by saying I have believed, so that the three abide together, since because thou hast believed thou hast hoped and because thou hast hoped thou hast loved. He calls on the soul sojourning in absence from the Lord, the sheep that had strayed and the son who died and returned to life to sing the verse with him.

Calvin weighs the two candidates for authorship, some ascribing the psalm to Hezekiah on his recovery from the sickness recorded of him and others to David after the rebellion of Absalom, and prefers the second, since the later verse in which the psalmist calls all men liars suits a betrayed king better than a man recovering from illness. He hears the abrupt opening as emphatic, a man intimating that he could find joy and repose nowhere but in God, and warns that our hearts wander after fruitless pleasures until God knits them to himself, and that those who have been heard but do not place themselves under his guidance have gained little from the experience of his grace. Gill grounds the love in the perfections of God’s nature and in the works of creation, providence and grace, redemption first among them, and denies that God is hard of hearing, since he listens when prayers are like the chattering of a crane or a swallow, or only sighs without a voice, and bows his ear as a nurse does to a child.

Spurgeon makes the declaration itself the point, since it was required under the law but never produced in a human heart except by grace, love being at once the sweetest of the graces and the surest evidence of salvation; he notes that the psalmist knows not only that he loves but why, and that when love can justify itself with a reason it is deep and abiding, so that although love is said to be blind, in loving God the affection has its eyes open. Henry calls the abrupt opening fitting, since a profession the heart is full of complies with the first and great commandment and God’s love of compassion toward us requires our love of complacency in him; and he finds in the inclined ear both readiness, God laying his ear to the mouth of prayer though it be whispered in groanings that cannot be uttered, and a wonderful condescension in the stooping, adding that as long as we continue living we must continue praying.

Clarke takes the psalm for a thanksgiving written after the captivity, that captivity being compared to death and the grave and the return called the land of the living; he reports that the Syriac supposes it written when Saul came to the mouth of the cave where David lay hidden, and that many, most of the fathers among them, referred the whole psalm to the passion and triumph of Christ. Against the objection that loving God for his benefits is mercenary he answers that no other love can flow from the creature to its Creator, that we love him because he first loved us, and that love begets love. On the inclined ear he pictures a suppliant so sick and weak that he could scarcely speak, to whose mouth the Lord bends down to catch every word, and concludes that a man who prays much will be emboldened to pray more, since none supplicate the throne of grace in vain.

Keil and Delitzsch call the psalm an anonymous thanksgiving rather than a supplication, sung with a fresh recollection of a deadly peril just got the better of and from the lips of an individual who distinguishes himself from the church; they note that the Greek version divided it at the tenth verse into two Hallelujah psalms while joining the two preceding into one, that its four strophes have corresponding openings, and that the late date of composition shows in the strong Aramaic colouring. Ellicott observes that the first verb has no object and that this poet is given to using verbs without one, so that besides the received reading two others are possible, I have longed that the Lord should hear, as the Syriac and Arabic take it, or I am well pleased that the Lord hears, as the Greek and Latin do; he also finds the second half of the following verse difficult, the literal text reading and in my days I will call, but there is none, and prefers to render it as the common phrase, in the day when I call.

debates: Who wrote it and when? Keil and Delitzsch leave it anonymous but date it late from its Aramaic colouring; Clarke places it after the captivity; Calvin decides for David after the rebellion of Absalom against those who name Hezekiah.

What does the first clause say? Ellicott reports two further renderings from the versions, that the poet longed for God to hear or was well pleased that he hears; Augustine, Spurgeon and Gill all keep the plain declaration of love and argue from it.

Is it mercenary to love God for his benefits? Clarke says no other love can flow from creature to Creator and that love begets love; Augustine makes hope the thing that inflames the love; Spurgeon holds that love able to give its reason is the stronger for it.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch note that the Greek version split this psalm in two at the tenth verse while joining the two psalms before it into one.
Augustine derives the whole triad from the verse, since because thou hast believed thou hast hoped, and because thou hast hoped thou hast loved.
Gill and Clarke both press the condescension of the bowed ear, Gill comparing a nurse stooping to a child and Clarke a suppliant too weak to speak above a whisper.
themes: love that can give its reason
a verb without an object
faith, hope and love in one line
an ear bowed to a whisper
praying as long as life lasts

3.pericope_label: The sorrows of death compassed me, and the pains of hell gat hold upon me: I found trouble and sorrow. Then called I upon the name of the Lord; O Lord, I beseech thee, deliver my soul. Gracious is the Lord, and righteous; yea, our God is merciful. The Lord preserveth the simple: I was brought low, and he helped me. Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the Lord hath dealt bountifully with thee

schools.summary: Gill reads the third verse typologically, applying it first to Christ, of whom he takes David to be a type, a man of sorrows surrounded with sorrow in the garden and dying the painful and accursed death of the cross, then to David himself when Saul and his men compassed him about and he had the sentence of death in himself, and then to any of God’s people who through a slavish fear of death are all their lifetime subject to bondage. He takes calling on the name to mean either calling on the Lord for speedy deliverance or calling in the name of the Messiah, the one Mediator, and notes that graciousness is what the psalmist found in the act of calling. The simple he defines as those of small understanding, whom several old versions call babes, men sensible of their want of wisdom who do not lean on what they have but commit themselves to the Lord, artless and easily imposed upon by designing men and therefore preserved from a total and final falling away, from gross errors and heresies, from the snares of the world and from the temptations of Satan. The rest he takes to be Christ, a cessation not from doing works but from depending on them, a deliverance from the curse of the law and the tyranny of sin, a peace broken in upon by temptation and desertion but returned to as the dove returned to the ark when it could find rest nowhere else.

Clarke renders the first phrase the cables or cords of death and offers several pictures for it, the bonds and fetters of a captivity, the cords by which a criminal is bound as he is led to execution, and the bandages in which the dead were wrapped with head, arms, body and limbs laced together; the second phrase he makes the straitnesses of the grave, since there was so little expectation of life that the psalmist speaks as one already condemned, executed and shut in the tomb, perhaps in one of the small niches where coffins were placed. He then attacks the supposition, drawn from the use of this psalm in the thanksgiving of women after a safe delivery, that the pain of childbirth equals for its duration the torments of the damned, calling it shockingly absurd since human nature could not endure the wrath of God for a moment and the body must first die, be decomposed and be rebuilt on indestructible principles before such punishment could be borne. He takes the simple for those meek and lowly of heart who feel the spirit of little children, over whom God sets a peculiar regard and gives his angels charge, and makes God the centre toward which all immortal spirits tend, everything separated from its centre being in a state of violence and unable, if intelligent, to be happy, though he allows that the rest here may more immediately mean the promised land, and finds in two forms in the verse a mark of the psalm’s late origin.

Ellicott prefers to emend the second phrase of the third verse, since the text as it stands gives the oppressions of the grave but a change in a single letter brings the clause into closer correspondence with the earlier psalm from which it is plainly borrowed and yields the nets of the grave; he would also keep one verb in both halves, so that the nets catch the psalmist and he in turn catches trouble and sorrow. He glosses the simple as the inexperienced in a good sense, as the word often is in the book of Proverbs, and notes that the Greek and Latin have babes. On the return to rest he adds the distinction that this repose is not the worldling’s serenity nor the sensualist’s security, and is quite unlike the fool’s address to his own soul in the parable, but is the repose of a quiet conscience and a trusting heart. Keil and Delitzsch pass over these verses without comment, reserving their note for the profession of faith that follows.

debates: What are the cords and pains of the third verse? Clarke reads captivity, execution and burial into them; Ellicott emends a letter to recover the nets of the grave from the psalm this one borrows from; Gill refers the whole verse to Christ and then to David.

Who are the simple that God preserves? Gill and Clarke both follow the versions that render babes or little ones, Gill making them the artless and Clarke the meek and lowly; Ellicott keeps it lexical, the inexperienced in a good sense.

What rest is the soul told to return to? Clarke makes God the centre to which all spirits tend, while allowing that the promised land may be the immediate sense; Gill makes it Christ and a cessation from depending on works; Ellicott defines it against the false securities it resembles.
outliers: Clarke calls it shockingly absurd to suppose, from the use of this psalm after childbirth, that the pain of delivery equals the torments of the damned.
Clarke finds a mark of the psalm’s late origin in two Chaldee forms in the seventh verse.
Gill compares the soul returning to its rest with the dove returning to the ark when it could find rest nowhere else.
themes: cords, nets and the straitness of the grave
a psalm borrowed from an older one
babes whom God preserves
a centre that spirits return to
rest that is not the fool’s security

8.pericope_label: For thou hast delivered my soul from death, mine eyes from tears, and my feet from falling. I will walk before the Lord in the land of the living. I believed, therefore have I spoken: I was greatly afflicted

schools.summary: Spurgeon calls the ninth verse the psalmist’s second resolution, to live as in the sight of God among the sons of men, since a man’s walk is his way of life and some live only as in the sight of their fellows, with an eye to human judgment and opinion, whereas the truly gracious man considers the presence of God and acts under his all-observing eye; he puts the difference in a sentence, that Thou God seest me is a far better influence than My master sees me. On the profession of faith he argues that he could not have spoken so but for his faith and would never have prayed nor been able to testify had faith not kept him alive, and that no man should speak about the things of God unless he believes, since the speech of the waverer is mischievous while the tongue of the believer is profitable and the most powerful speech ever uttered has come from a heart fully persuaded. Henry notes the same division of the psalm without contesting it, passes on the name it acquired as the Martyr’s psalm, finds three confessions in what follows, of faith, of fear and of gratitude, and takes the first as the ground of the speech: what David believed included the assurance given him by the prophet that he should exchange his crook for a sceptre, and having endured much hardship in that belief he spoke, to God in prayer and praise, to himself when he told his soul to return to its rest, and to others, telling his friends what his hope was though it exasperated the king against him. Those who believe with the heart, he adds, must confess with the mouth.

Gill distributes the deliverance across three deaths, a bodily one when the psalmist was surrounded by an army, in enemy hands at Gath and driven out by his own son, a spiritual one since regeneration is a passing from death to life, and an eternal one which is the just wages of sin. He grounds the walking before the Lord in a comparison, another man’s walking with God being explained by the apostle as pleasing him and several old versions rendering the clause I will please the Lord, and takes the land of the living for this world or the church, though he reports that Jewish commentators find in it the land of Canaan, itself a type of where glorified saints dwell for ever. He calls the division of the psalm at this point groundless, unsupported by the original or the Targum and plainly against the connection with what precedes; and he fills in what the belief contained, not merely that God is but that this God was gracious and his own, bound to him by a covenant ordered in all things and sure, noting that the apostle applies the words to himself and his fellow ministers.

Clarke reads the threefold deliverance as rescue, joy and safe footing, a life snatched from destruction, sorrow turned into joy, and a man taken out of a land of snares and pitfalls into a plain path; he is pleased at how nearly the old English renderings come to the Hebrew and quotes both an Anglo-Saxon version and an old Psalter that has, he took my saule fra dede, my eghen fra teres, my fete fra slippyng. In the verb of the ninth verse he hears a deliberate setting out, the eyes brightened so that he can see, the feet strengthened so that he can walk, the soul alive so that he can walk with the living. He reports that the Greek, Latin, Ethiopic, Arabic and Anglo-Saxon versions all close the psalm at the ninth verse and begin a new one with the profession of faith, a division the Hebrew, Chaldee and Syriac do not acknowledge; and on that profession he keeps the struggle in view, since the promises were believed throughout but confidence was hard to maintain, the afflictions being oppressive and of long standing. He adds the curiosity that the letters Hebrew grammarians call heemantic are taken from the first word of the tenth verse.
Ellicott keeps to the last clause of the eighth verse, preferring stumbling to falling and pointing to the older psalm from which the phrase comes.

debates: Where does the psalm end? Clarke reports that five old versions close it at the ninth verse and begin a new psalm with the profession of faith; Gill calls that division groundless and against the connection; Henry notes it without contesting it and records the name the second part acquired.
What death was the soul delivered from? Gill distinguishes a bodily, a spiritual and an eternal death; Clarke keeps it to the rescue of a life from destruction.

Why does the psalmist speak? Henry and Spurgeon both make faith the ground of the speech, Henry directing it to God, to the soul and to friends, Spurgeon warning that the speech of a waverer is mischievous; Clarke stresses how hard the confidence was to hold.
outliers: Clarke quotes an Anglo-Saxon version and an old Psalter on this verse: he took my saule fra dede, my eghen fra teres, my fete fra slippyng.
Spurgeon contrasts two motives for a watched life, that Thou God seest me is a far better influence than My master sees me.
Henry passes on the name the second half of the psalm acquired, the Martyr’s psalm, from the verse about the death of the saints.
themes: three deaths in one deliverance
a walk under an all-observing eye
one psalm or two
faith as the ground of speech
a crook exchanged for a sceptre

11.pericope_label: I said in my haste, All men are liars. What shall I render unto the Lord for all his benefits toward me? I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord. I will pay my vows unto the Lord now in the presence of all his people. Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints

schools.summary: Spurgeon calls the paying of vows the psalmist’s third resolution and the beginning of its performance, since good resolutions cannot be carried out too speedily, vows become debts and debts should be paid, and there is no more shame in having witnesses to a holy vow than to the payment of a just debt, this being a way of showing that a man is not ashamed of his Lord and a benefit to those who look on; from there he turns to the secret disciples and asks what they say to the verse. On the death of the saints he takes the verse to explain why the psalmist was not suffered to die, and suggests the song was meant to remind families of the mercies received when a member of the household had been sore sick and was restored.

Gill grants that lying is common to man and that there is a natural propensity to it, but denies the charge can be universal, since those who have received grace put it off with the rest of the old man, and holds that however degenerate the age some did not deserve the imputation, so that the psalmist on cool reflection owned he had spoken rashly, in a passion and under temptation, and repented of it. On the question what to render he notes that the psalmist looks only to the Lord as the author of his mercies and says nothing of his own merits or of the men who were instruments of good to him, being at a loss how to make any return but determined to express a grateful sense of what he had received. He rejects the eucharistic reading of the cup and the reading that makes it a cup of afflictions or martyrdom, preferring an offering of praise for temporal and spiritual salvation, in allusion to the master of a family who takes up a cup at the close of a meal and gives thanks; and he makes the vows the resolutions taken in the time of trouble and now made good publicly before the assembled people as witnesses. On the death of the saints he lets them die like other men, since Christ has abolished death as a punishment and taken away its curse and sting without taking away the thing itself, which remains for their good.

Clarke collects the renderings of the phrase in my haste, which appears as in my light, in my excess or ecstasy, in my giddiness, in my fear or tremor, and in old English versions as when I was beside myself, and gives the sense as the moment when passion got the better of reason and the man looked not at God but at his afflictions and the impossibility of human relief. On the charge itself he is harsher than Gill, holding that the whole of man is a lie, falsity being diffused through his nature so that he is imposed on by others and imposes in his turn, with no dependence to be placed on any until God converts the heart; he supports it with verses on what commerce would become if each could see another’s heart and with a proverb that men live half the year by deceit and art and the other half by art and deceit, then asks who gives mankind this bad character and answers, man. He describes the custom of the cup of blessing with its benediction of the Maker of the world who created the fruit of the vine, but leans toward the libation offering, since the closing verses suggest a man standing in the temple with his offerings, and notes that cup often denotes abundance, of misery or of happiness. He turns the calling on the name into an argument about debt, since the only return God asks is that we ask for more, so that the reason never to trouble a fellow mortal again is that we have had so many favours already while the reason to claim the utmost salvation of God is that we are so far in his debt, every attempt to discharge it only increasing it, and yet debtor and creditor are both pleased and both happy in each other. On the last verse he reports the construction that the saints are too precious in the Lord’s sight to be lightly given over to death.

Keil and Delitzsch infer from what the poet has experienced that the saints are under God’s most especial providence, note that he chooses a pathetic form of the word for death, and apply to that word the observation that what is precious we do not part with easily: the death of his saints is no trifling matter with God, he does not lightly suffer it to come about, and he does not suffer his own to be torn away from him by death. Ellicott renders the cup clause lift up and takes the cup for the drink offering that accompanied festival celebrations, while reporting the rival views that find the Passover cup, this psalm having been sung as part of the festal group, or the figurative sense of cup as portion or lot. On the last verse he asks why the thought of death should intrude at this moment and answers that a recent deliverance from death is in view, the psalm reading naturally as a thanksgiving for the safety, perhaps the victory, of the survivors of some battle, in which a grateful community would remember its dead.

debates: Are all men liars? Gill limits the charge, since grace puts off lying and some in every age do not deserve the imputation, and takes the psalmist to have retracted it; Clarke widens it, holding that the whole of man is a lie and no dependence can be placed on any until God converts the heart.

What is the cup of salvation? Gill makes it an offering of praise and rejects both the eucharistic and the martyrdom readings; Clarke describes the cup of blessing but prefers the libation offering; Ellicott takes the drink offering and reports the Passover cup and the figurative portion as rivals.

Why is the death of the saints called precious? Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke both read it as God valuing their lives too highly to give them up lightly, which Spurgeon applies to the psalmist’s own escape; Gill keeps their death real and makes it good for them; Ellicott sets the verse against a recent deliverance and a community remembering its dead.
outliers: Clarke argues that the only return God asks is that we ask for more, so that every attempt to discharge the debt increases it, while debtor and creditor are both pleased in each other.
Clarke quotes a proverb that men live half the year by deceit and art and the other half by art and deceit, then asks who gives mankind this bad character and answers, man.
Ellicott suggests the psalm is a thanksgiving for the survivors of a battle, whose grateful community would naturally remember its dead.
themes: a charge retracted on reflection
a cup lifted at the close of a meal
vows paid before witnesses
a debt that grows as it is paid
a death God does not lightly permit

16.pericope_label: O Lord, truly I am thy servant; I am thy servant, and the son of thine handmaid: thou hast loosed my bonds. I will offer to thee the sacrifice of thanksgiving, and will call upon the name of the Lord. I will pay my vows unto the Lord now in the presence of all his people, in the courts of the Lord’s house, in the midst of thee, O Jerusalem. Praise ye the Lord

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes the grounds of servanthood, since a man is God’s servant by creation and under obligation for providential favours, but the psalmist is one by the grace of God which made him willing, and in reality rather than in name, unlike those who say Lord, Lord and do not the will of God; he takes the repetition as a confirmation and a mark of heartiness, and denies that anything meritorious is claimed, holding rather that standing in that character obliges a man to serve the Lord only and gives him ground to expect protection. On the sacrifice of thanksgiving he lists what it is offered for, deliverance from affliction and death, the loosing of bonds in every sense, and all mercies temporal and spiritual, and holds such sacrifices to be according to the will of God and well pleasing when offered through Christ and in faith, more acceptable than all the ceremonial sacrifices, so that the psalmist determines to offer this and not those. The courts of the house he treats as an explanation of the earlier phrase about the presence of all the people, meaning the assembly of the saints gathered at the door of the tabernacle and in its courts.

Clarke hears the profession as the language of a household, the speaker declaring that he lives with God, for him and to him as a willing domestic, the son of a handmaid and so like one born in the house of a woman already his master’s property; and he supplies the legal picture behind it, of a servant entitled to freedom in the year of release who refuses to go out and has his ear bored to the door-post as evidence that he stays by his own consent, to continue there for ever. He reads the closing verses historically, holding it most probable that the psalm celebrates the deliverance from Babylon, so that it is no wonder to find the writer intent on performing the rites of his religion in the temple at Jerusalem, a building burnt with fire and then reviving out of its ruins after its service had been wholly interrupted for nearly four-score years. He takes the writer to speak as one already present in the city offering his vowed sacrifices, and closes by reporting that most of the psalm has been applied to Christ and his Church and so taken as prophetic, an accommodation he calls innocent and very edifying and the interpretation the old Psalter gives of the whole.

Ellicott draws from the mention of the handmaid the inference that not the speaker only but his family stood within the covenant, and observes that the mother is named instead of the father, as is very commonly done in the East. Keil and Delitzsch print the closing verses without comment.

debates: What kind of servant is meant? Gill separates the servanthood of creation and providence from the servanthood of grace, which makes a man willing; Clarke makes it the bondservant who refuses his freedom and has his ear bored to the door-post; Ellicott takes the handmaid clause to bring the whole family within the covenant.

What occasion do the closing verses fix? Clarke reads them as a return from Babylon to a temple only then reviving out of its ruins; Gill keeps to the assembly of saints in the courts of the house without dating it.

How far should the psalm be applied to Christ? Clarke reports that most of it has been so applied and taken as prophetic, calls the accommodation innocent and edifying, and credits the old Psalter with reading the whole that way; Gill reaches Christ through the sacrifice of thanksgiving offered in faith rather than by prophecy.
outliers: Clarke explains the bored ear from the law of the servant who, entitled to freedom in the year of release, refused to leave his master’s house.
Ellicott notes that the mother rather than the father is named, as is very commonly done in the East.
Clarke dates the psalm to a temple service that had been wholly interrupted for nearly four-score years.
themes: a servant twice declared
an ear bored to the door-post
a family inside the covenant
thanksgiving preferred to ceremony
vows paid in the courts
